article.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
article.summary:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

article.title: COP31 went up in flames over fossil fuels — it sends an important message
article.summary:
Anyone hoping for bold action on climate change has many reasons to be disappointed by the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31, which concluded in a dramatic overtime session on 22 November.
After gathering for nearly two weeks in the beach resort city of Antalya, Turkey, in what will probably be the hottest year on record, representatives from nearly all the world’s countries failed to agree on a plan to tackle climate change.
Almost 100 nations walked out without signing a ‘cover decision’ — a non-binding statement meant to push for ambitious action — because the document did not call on the world to transition away from fossil fuels.
The last COP climate talk to break down this badly was the Copenhagen summit in 2009.
But when language targeting fossil fuels disappeared from the draft cover decision after lobbying by oil-rich nations, a coalition of around 90 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, rejected the agreement.

The mainly Muslim Rohingya – described as the ‘world’s most persecuted minority’ – make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

article.title: Migrants using knives to slash roofs of lorries as they cross into Britain undetected - before brazenly posting about it on TikTok
article.summary:
Migrants are using knives to slash their way through lorries and trucks in the latest tactic to illegally sneak into Britain.
Social media footage shows male migrants brazenly showing off their blades in the back of UK-bound lorries.
Other migrants have filmed videos showing where they have slashed through roofs to sneak into lorries.
It comes after footage earlier this year showed migrants jumping from the roof of an HGV after arriving from France.
On June 26, a Malian migrant showed off a knife he used to cut a hole in a roof.

article.title: Danish top court’s ‘ghetto law’ ruling supports hardline immigration policy
article.summary:
The country’s top court said eviction of ‘non-Western’ families did not constitute discrimination.
Denmark’s top court has ruled that the eviction of “non-Western” tenants from a social housing estate under the country’s “ghetto law” was not discriminatory.
The country’s “ghetto law” housing legislation, adopted in 2018, allows for the ⁠relocation of residents from areas in which more than half of residents are “non-Western”.
It requires social housing estates to change the social mix by renting at least 60 percent of homes at market rates by 2030.
The 2018 “ghetto law” is aimed at combatting segregation and “parallel societies” in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, according to the government.

article.title: Ms. Rachel Shows Support for Families at NYC Immigration Court
article.summary:
Ms. Rachel met with children appearing without an attorney at federal youth immigration court in Manhattan on Monday.
“Kids representing themselves in immigration court is so wrong.
He’s 9 years old!” Ms. Rachel wrote in the caption.
Stop the cruelty!”When Ms. Rachel asked Angel to write a list of things he wanted for Christmas, he asked for an immigration lawyer.
Ms. Rachel stopped by the court alongside Congressman-elect Brad Lander, according to ABC 7.

article.title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah visit: India to give $1.62bn economic package
article.summary:
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

article.title: Countries that thrive on global cooperation must help sustain it
article.summary:
“For thriving states, international peace and stability are not a luxury.
The prime minister’s concept of thriving states offers a way to think about their response.
The Global North and the Global South tell us little about which countries can work together on a particular problem.
Their diplomatic access and financial resources are increasingly necessary to sustain functions that international institutions struggle to perform consistently.
The next step is to organise sustained cooperation among willing thriving states.

article.title: How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth
article.summary:
The US, China and Russia are vying for Africa’s mineral wealth, raising questions about who stands to benefitShare How the US, China and Russia are competing for Africa’s mineral wealth on social mediaFrom cobalt mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to lithium deposits in Mali and uranium reserves in Niger, Africa’s mineral wealth is becoming an increasingly important arena of competition between the United States, China and Russia.
China dominates several critical mineral supply chains, while Russia has expanded its influence through security partnerships, particularly in the Sahel.
But as foreign powers compete for access, what do African countries stand to gain?
China has spent years investing in African mining, processing and infrastructure.
As Washington, Beijing and Moscow compete for Africa’s mineral wealth, the real test for African countries may be not which global power wins the race, but how much of the wealth they can retain.
